paper_metadata.title: Scheduling process of quantum circuits to optimize tasks execution on quantum computers

summary: The paper proposes a quantum circuit scheduler that batches multiple user circuits into a single execution on cloud QPUs (IBM Eagle/Heron and Amazon Braket IQM Garnet). Using 10 benchmark algorithms, scheduled execution reduced average runtime from 80 s (individual runs) to 20 s and lowered execution cost from $44.40 to $11.10 on Braket (~75%) and from $363.08 to $23.27 on IBM (~93.53%), while maintaining similar output distributions (≈7% Wasserstein distance on average).

experiments.description: Circuit scheduling experiment combining multiple gate-based quantum circuits into a single execution on IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket, evaluated on several benchmark algorithms and compared against individual executions.

algorithm.variant: Quantum circuit scheduling / circuit unification for multiple user circuits

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Multiple independent circuits are mapped to disjoint qubit subsets within a single scheduled circuit; e.g., a 3-qubit circuit assigned qubits 0-2 and a 4-qubit circuit assigned qubits 3-6.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize queue waiting time and execution cost by combining multiple circuits into one execution while preserving individual circuit outputs.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Disjoint qubit allocation; circuits are scheduled FIFO within a cycle until available qubits are filled; results are unscheduled by splitting measured bitstrings back into per-circuit outputs.

problem_instance.description: Public benchmark quantum circuits from Zenodo used to validate scheduling across providers.

dataset_specification.description: Circuit implementations for Berstein-Vazirani, Deutsch-Jozsa, Full Adder, Grover, Kickback, Phase Estimation, Quantum Walk, Shor, Simon, and TSP

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Circuits are adapted to provider connectivity and gate sets during transpilation; scheduled circuits are assigned to specific qubit ranges before execution.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison of scheduled vs individual executions on IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket; noise impact assessed using Wasserstein distance between output probability distributions.

hardware.transpilation_target: Provider-specific connectivity and gate sets; circuits transpiled before execution

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Unscheduling: split combined measurement results into per-circuit outputs and store with unique identifiers.
implementation_details.total_execution_time: Average individual executions: 80 s; scheduled execution: 20 s
implementation_details.quantum_execution_time: Scheduled circuit execution time close to the deepest circuit time

speedup_claims.conditions: Average wall-clock execution time reduced from 80 s to 20 s using circuit scheduling
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a practical runtime reduction, not an asymptotic complexity result.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: individual circuit executions on Amazon Braket
speedup_claims.conditions: Average across the tested benchmark circuits
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported as average reduction in execution cost, not a theoretical speedup.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: individual circuit executions on IBM Quantum
speedup_claims.conditions: Average across the tested benchmark circuits
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported as average reduction in execution cost, not a theoretical speedup.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not applicable; the work evaluates scheduling efficiency rather than algorithmic speedup.
limiting_factors: No comparison with classical scheduling frameworks for quantum workloads
Performance gains measured only as cost and queue-time reduction, not computational advantage
Results depend on cloud-provider pricing and queue structure rather than algorithmic complexity

notes: Hardware type is reported as IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket QPUs; specific IBM devices are superconducting. The paper does not report exact qubit counts for each experiment in a single consolidated value, only device capacities (20, 127, 133, 156 qubits) and that circuits are assigned to available qubits.
Circuit depth is not numerically reported; only transpilation and 'deepest circuit' are mentioned.
Speedup order is inferred as none_proven because the paper reports practical cost/time reduction but no asymptotic complexity claim.
The paper does not claim quantum advantage; it proposes a scheduling system to combine multiple circuits in one job.
Reported improvements (execution time 80 s → 20 s and cost reductions of 75% on Braket and 93.53% on IBM) arise from batching circuits, not from a faster quantum algorithm.

algorithm.variant: Noise validation for scheduled quantum circuit execution

problem_formulation.objective_function: Quantify similarity between probability distributions from scheduled and individually executed circuits.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: None beyond scheduled circuit partitioning and result unscheduling.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Statistical comparison of scheduled vs individual executions; reported distances per algorithm and provider.
